boundary: This is an educational design, not a medical tool. NICE guideline NG87 covers recognising, diagnosing and managing ADHD, including medication and non-drug treatment, and it is the clinical reference; nothing in this application treats ADHD or replaces that care. ADHD presents differently in different people (CDC notes symptoms and support needs change over the lifetime), so every support below is optional and adjustable.

evidenceKey.moderate: Meta-analytic or repeated experimental evidence with notable heterogeneity, or strong evidence for a deficit with a design inference drawn from it.
evidenceKey.promising: Some evidence, but small, indirect, child-only or not tested in adults with ADHD.
evidenceKey.practice: Sensible practice or guideline recommendation without direct outcome evidence.

items.feature: One clear next action, resume exactly where you stopped, and a 'park a thought' box
items.finding: After an interruption, people must re-retrieve their suspended goal; explicit, blatant environmental cues of the previous action shortened resumption, while subtle cues were no better than none. Separately, CDC lists staying organised and completing lengthy tasks as common adult ADHD difficulties.

sources.title: Altmann & Trafton (2002). Memory for goals: an activation-based model. Cognitive Science 26, 39–83
Trafton & Altmann (2005). Huh, what was I doing? How people use environmental cues after an interruption. HFES
CDC — ADHD in Adults

items.feature: Lessons and build guides split into short, learner-paced steps, one focus at a time
items.finding: A meta-analysis of 56 investigations found a significant segmenting effect (small to medium) on retention and transfer when instruction is broken into learner-paced segments.

sources.title: Rey et al. (2019). A meta-analysis of the segmenting effect. Educational Psychology Review 31, 389–419

items.feature: Low working-memory load: the equation, the controls and the readout are on one screen; nothing to hold in your head between pages
items.finding: A meta-analysis of 38 studies found moderate working-memory deficits in adults with ADHD in both phonological and visuospatial domains. Reducing unnecessary load is a design inference from this, not a tested intervention. Computerised working-memory training showed only a small cognitive effect and no significant effect on symptoms in adults, so the app does not include 'brain training'.

sources.title: Alderson, Kasper, Hudec & Patros (2013). ADHD and working memory in adults: a meta-analytic review. Neuropsychology 27(3), 287–302
Elbe et al. (2023). Computerized cognitive interventions for adults with ADHD: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Neuropsychology 37(5), 519–530

items.feature: Visual first, with cues on what matters and no decorative animation
items.finding: Signalling the essential elements improved learning outcomes (d ≈ .38) across a meta-analysis; Mayer's coherence and multimedia principles favour words plus relevant pictures and excluding extraneous material.

sources.title: Alpizar, Adesope & Wong (2020). A meta-analysis of signaling principle in multimedia learning environments. ETR&D 68, 2095–2119
Mayer (2020). Multimedia Learning, 3rd ed. — principle summary

items.feature: Predict before you see the experiment
items.finding: Students who only watched physics demonstrations understood the concept no better than students who did not see them; students who predicted the outcome first showed significantly greater understanding. A later replication in astronomy found weaker, topic-dependent effects.

sources.title: Crouch, Fagen, Callan & Mazur (2004). Classroom demonstrations: learning tools or entertainment? Am. J. Phys. 72, 835
UNL DBER replication summary (2014)

items.feature: Explain-it-back and the Review page (retrieval practice)
items.finding: Practice testing beats restudying: Adesope et al. (2017) pooled 272 effect sizes (g ≈ 0.61 fixed, 0.70 random effects); Rowland (2014) found g = 0.50. Classroom and laboratory effects were similar.

sources.title: Adesope, Trevisan & Sundararajan (2017). Rethinking the use of tests: a meta-analysis of practice testing. Review of Educational Research 87(3), 659–701
Review of meta-analytic evidence on testing (PMC)

items.finding: A quantitative synthesis of 839 assessments in 317 experiments found that spaced practice improves retention and that the best gap grows with how long you need to remember. The specific interval ladder used here is a practical choice, not an optimum derived from that paper.

sources.title: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks. Psychological Bulletin 132(3), 354–380

items.feature: Informative feedback (expected results, oracles, model answers) instead of points, badges or praise
items.finding: A meta-analysis of 435 studies found a medium average feedback effect (d = 0.48) with large heterogeneity; feedback that carries more information is more effective, while praise, rewards and punishment have low effects.

sources.title: Wisniewski, Zierer & Hattie (2020). The power of feedback revisited. Frontiers in Psychology 10, 3087

items.feature: An if–then plan for your next session on the dashboard
items.finding: If–then plans (implementation intentions) had a medium-to-large average effect on goal attainment (d = 0.65, 94 tests); a 2024 synthesis of 642 tests gives smaller bias-corrected estimates. In children with ADHD they improved response inhibition; they have not been well tested in adults with ADHD.

sources.title: Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis. Adv. Exp. Soc. Psychol. 38, 69–119
Gawrilow & Gollwitzer (2008). Implementation intentions facilitate response inhibition in children with ADHD. Cognitive Therapy and Research 32, 261–280
APSARD — implementation intentions not yet studied in adults with ADHD

items.feature: Assistance levels (full → guided → independent): code and hints fade as you progress
items.finding: Guidance that helps novices can become redundant and even harmful for more experienced learners (expertise reversal); fading worked steps, especially adaptively, supports the move to independent problem solving.

sources.title: Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller (2003). The expertise reversal effect. Educational Psychologist 38, 23–31
Kalyuga, Rikers & Paas (2012). Educational implications of expertise reversal effects. Educ. Psychol. Rev. 24, 313–337

items.feature: Visible mastery: the validation ladder, honest completion, and progress tied to real checks
items.finding: In a systematic review of college students with ADHD and/or learning disorders, academic regulation, academic self-efficacy, emotional regulation, ADHD symptoms and integration predicted GPA and retention. Reviews of university students with ADHD highlight executive function and metacognition as key barriers.

sources.title: Stevens, Abu-Ramadan & Hartung (2022). Promoting academic success in college students with ADHD and LD: a systematic review. J. Am. Coll. Health 70(8)
Álvarez-Godos, Ferreira & Vieira (2023). A systematic review of actions aimed at university students with ADHD. Front. Psychol. 14
Pagespetit et al. ADHD and academic performance in college students: a systematic review. J. Atten. Disord., doi:10.1177/10870547241306554

items.feature: Your own controls: text size, light/dark, reduced motion, read-aloud, focus mode
items.finding: UDL Guidelines 3.0 recommend offering choices and letting learners customise how information is displayed (Consideration 1.1), with multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression.

sources.title: CAST (2024). Universal Design for Learning Guidelines 3.0

items.feature: Optional focus sessions and breaks — no fixed Pomodoro, nothing locks
items.finding: There is no strong evidence for a particular session length or break schedule for adults with ADHD. The timer is therefore optional, the length is yours, and ending a session never blocks you.

items.feature: Academic, computer-aided supports rather than generic behaviour rewards
items.finding: In a meta-analysis of school-based interventions (60 studies), academic interventions such as computer-aided instruction had the largest effects on academic outcomes. The samples were children, so transfer to university students is uncertain.

sources.title: DuPaul, Eckert & Vilardo (2012). The effects of school-based interventions for ADHD: a meta-analysis 1996–2010. School Psychology Review 41(4), 387–412

references.title: NICE NG87 — Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management
